A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CodeChemist research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including figures, tables, equations, and prompts, are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revision and reformatting.

before.justification: V1 reports original code-generation benchmark results, sampling and oracle-generation ablations, runtime measurements, and a CodeChemist–S* combination experiment.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark comparisons and additional adaptive-selection, efficiency, language-generalization, code-style, and failure-analysis results, including appendix experiments.

M1.justification: V1 always constructs high-resource test oracles. V2 first clusters target-language candidates by execution behavior and AST similarity, selects through in-language voting when uncertainty is low, and constructs cross-language oracles otherwise (Section 3.3; Algorithm 1). This adds a substantive routing and selection component while retaining hedged sampling and oracle-based scoring.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates Python, Lua, C++, and Java across the three retained benchmarks. V2 adds R and Julia on Ag-LiveCodeBench-X, Rust generation using C++ references on MultiPL-HumanEval, and a C# class-generation case on RepoClassBench Task 56 (Appendix B.5). These expand language coverage and introduce generation using repository context.

E2.justification: V2 adds Self-Debugging to the reported comparisons. MultiPL-MBPP and Ag-LiveCodeBench-X, compared only against Vanilla in v1, additionally receive Majority Voting, LLM Judge, and S* comparisons. Appendix B.4 also introduces evaluated CodeT and MBR-Exec comparisons on MultiPL-HumanEval; CodeT's earlier citation alone was not such an evaluation.

E3.justification: Timing comparisons change from Qwen-3B to Qwen-32B and add token usage. Oracle ablations replace Qwen-3B with Qwen-1.5B; new settings include additional sampling temperatures, candidate-count sweeps, Thinking Mode, and five-point code-style judging. The stated DeepSeek version changes from V3.1 to V3, without establishing whether experiments were rerun. Core benchmark sizes and the ten-candidate hedged-sampling budget remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V1 primarily ablates sampling strategy and reference-program count. V2 expands these analyses with direct oracle generation and alternative source languages, and adds adaptive-selection ablation, candidate/test-count sensitivity, consensus-rate analysis, conditional failure analysis, code-style assessment, and a repository-level case study (Tables 3–6 and 13; Figure 4; Appendices B–C). These test substantial new questions about selection, efficiency, reliability, and applicability.

E5.justification: Both versions report five differently seeded evaluations and p-values below 0.05 for selected models. V2 Appendix B.1 specifies full-evaluation repetitions and paired t-tests against the corresponding Vanilla baseline, whereas v1 Appendix A leaves the pairing and comparator unspecified. This refines statistical reporting without reporting an increase in runs.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive comparator, language, ablation, efficiency, style, and failure results. Table 1 replaces Qwen-1.5B C++/Java scores of 52.2/69.6 with 55.3/70.3 under the revised method. Figure 1 changes Qwen-14B's Ag-LiveCodeBench-X C++ Vanilla score from 31.6 to 30.6. Many other Ag-LiveCodeBench-X results are retained graphically, while MultiPL-MBPP results for Qwen-7B/14B, Llama-3B, and GPT-4o mini are omitted.

T1.justification: V2 Section 3.3 introduces execution and AST cluster counts and formally defines a binary uncertainty indicator through their threshold conditions. This is a new mathematical definition supporting adaptive selection. The existing softmax and pass-rate scoring formulas remain substantively unchanged, and neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion redefine CodeChemist as an uncertainty-aware adaptive framework, making selective avoidance of costly or misleading transfer a central contribution absent from v1. The training-free functional-transfer claim remains. V2 also newly claims that its Lua score of 50.5 surpasses a reported leaderboard best of 43.0 (Figure 1).

C2.justification: V2 adds the spurious-consensus rationale for AST clustering, explanations of adaptive computation and oracle noise, and an interpretation linking failures to source-model problem-solving limits. New Section 6 explicitly limits applicability for language-specific non-functional properties, tasks difficult even in the source language, and repository-level generation beyond the single case study. V1 lacks these substantive qualifications.

D1.justification: V2 newly provides a code-access link, execution CPU specifications, clustering thresholds, and detailed cross-language input conversion and output normalization, including type tags, container handling, and numerical tolerance (Appendix A.2). These substantially improve implementation documentation beyond v1's hardware, sampling, and prompt details. The normalization disclosure alone does not establish that the underlying handling changed.

R1.justification: The related-work framework largely remains, but v2 adds GenX and Epicoder discussion and citations supporting new baselines, clustering, and repository evaluation. Section 2.1 also recharacterizes Bridge-C from an inference-based prompting approach in v1 to a framework generating alignment-training data. These are limited substantive changes within the retained research positioning.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites and reorganizes the abstract, method narrative, experimental discussion, and conclusion. Method subsections are reordered, the algorithm moves to Appendix A.1, computational efficiency receives its own section, and v1 Appendices A–C are regrouped within Appendix B. The title and affiliation information also change.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one-column to two-column layout. The workflow diagram is redrawn for adaptive selection, Ag-LiveCodeBench-X results are also displayed as a new bar chart, and efficiency and sampling-budget plots are added. Benchmark tables are merged and expanded, new analysis tables appear, and retained prompt boxes are reflowed across two pages.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important evidential and reproducibility gaps: it replaces Vanilla-only comparisons on two benchmarks with competing methods, tests the adaptive gate's accuracy and cost, documents cross-language execution handling, and states concrete failure boundaries. These substantially strengthen the paper. Reduced MBPP model reporting and unreconciled numerical prose remain weaknesses—for example, Section 4.2 retains the 51.7% C++ gain despite Table 1's revised 55.3 versus 34.4—but do not outweigh the improvements.
